head.citation-title: Long-term influence of carbonation curing on external (Na⁺, Mg²⁺) sulfate attack in metakaolin-based geopolymer concretes
head.abstracts: © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.Sulfate attack causes concrete degradation, characterized by cracking, increased permeability, and loss of mechanical strength, resulting from chemical interactions with the cementitious matrix. Research has sought to reduce the porosity of geopolymers as a strategy to minimize these damages. Previous studies on Portland cement composites subjected to carbonation curing indicated improvements in resistance to sodium and magnesium sulfates, attributed to pore refinement. Unlike these previous approaches, this research aimed to evaluate the application of this curing technique in geopolymers exposed to sulfate environments, exploring its effects on the physical and mechanical properties of concrete. After prolonged exposure, carbonation curing did not prevent sulfate attack, but it mitigated the harmful effects of magnesium sulfates on the geopolymers. This curing technique promoted the partial removal of Mg⁺ ions from the MgSO₄ solution and favored the formation of protective phases, such as MgCO₃. Compressive strength was preserved throughout the tests and exceeded that of conventionally cured concrete by 28.10%. In a medium with Na₂SO₄, carbonation curing proved ineffective and even presented partially adverse effects. Compressive strength was reduced by 10.14%. However, the values remained equivalent to conventionally cured samples after 546 days of exposure to sodium sulfates. Thus, the study demonstrated that carbonation curing can increase the longevity of geopolymer concretes in environments with MgSO₄, while in environments with Na₂SO₄, this technique did not contribute to mitigating the deleterious action of sodium sulfates.

coredata.dc:description: Sulfate attack causes concrete degradation, characterized by cracking, increased permeability, and loss of mechanical strength, resulting from chemical interactions with the cementitious matrix. Research has sought to reduce the porosity of geopolymers as a strategy to minimize these damages. Previous studies on Portland cement composites subjected to carbonation curing indicated improvements in resistance to sodium and magnesium sulfates, attributed to pore refinement. Unlike these previous approaches, this research aimed to evaluate the application of this curing technique in geopolymers exposed to sulfate environments, exploring its effects on the physical and mechanical properties of concrete. After prolonged exposure, carbonation curing did not prevent sulfate attack, but it mitigated the harmful effects of magnesium sulfates on the geopolymers. This curing technique promoted the partial removal of Mg⁺ ions from the MgSO₄ solution and favored the formation of protective phases, such as MgCO₃. Compressive strength was preserved throughout the tests and exceeded that of conventionally cured concrete by 28.10%. In a medium with Na₂SO₄, carbonation curing proved ineffective and even presented partially adverse effects. Compressive strength was reduced by 10.14%. However, the values remained equivalent to conventionally cured samples after 546 days of exposure to sodium sulfates. Thus, the study demonstrated that carbonation curing can increase the longevity of geopolymer concretes in environments with MgSO₄, while in environments with Na₂SO₄, this technique did not contribute to mitigating the deleterious action of sodium sulfates.
coredata.dc:title: Long-term influence of carbonation curing on external (Na⁺, Mg²⁺) sulfate attack in metakaolin-based geopolymer concretes
